## (00:00) Isolation After _Blurryface_[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**Zane Lowe: This is the Batcave.**

Tyler Joseph: I've never really shown anyone this spot.

**ZL: Thanks for having us. Thanks for welcoming us. It's good to see you.**

TJ: Thanks for coming all the way to my place.

**ZL: It's a pleasure. It's lovely to be here. It's my first time, actually, in this part in the Midwest. Being out here, I realized, wow, isolation plays such a big part in your creative spirit, right?**

TJ: The isolation helps when creating something. I think that people would assume that the pressure of making another record to follow something that was considered a big moment for us in our career would be the pressure, when really it's the tiny comments that I think about.

TJ: Like when a friend's mom says, “I love your last record. I could just press play and listen to the whole thing as I worked out.” Something tiny like that, when I'm working on a song, will all of a sudden, like, “Can they work out to this?” It's the tiny little comments about the music and the decisions made in it that -- if I let too much of that in -- it can completely affect whether I turn left or right.

**ZL: Well, look, it's really great to be here, man, in your studio -- in your space where this new album has been made. I know that this is a particularly intense moment for us to catch up. Because normally what happens is, I catch up with an artist like yourself after a few weeks of decompression when the album’s done.**

**ZL: But I sort of snuck up on you -- and did this deliberately. Because when I heard the music, the idea of coming here and seeing you the day the album got done, that seed was planted. Because I realized that you had gone so deep in on the ideas, the concepts, and the entire complete thought of this album. I wanted to get you at its most raw. That's literally right now, right?**

TJ: Right now. Yeah, I'm pretty tired. Every moment away from a song is very valuable because the fresh ears aspect of it.

**ZL: How was that break that you took? Necessary?**

TJ: It was very necessary. A lot of the last album cycle, there was a lot of traveling.

**ZL: Well, you caught lightning in a bottle. I mean, you had to, right? It was -- you had to go. You had to go, go, go.**

TJ: Yeah. The schedule was very unpredictable. You know, “This is the next thing we need to do to capitalize on the momentum.” This time around I'm looking forward to a little more structure. We know what to expect a little bit more, which is fantastic.

**ZL: And yet you find yourself -- from what I've heard of this album, which is the whole thing thus far -- is that you have chosen this opportunity to dive _deeper_.**

TJ: I love stories. I love being able to dive into a story and write from that perspective. A lot of my writing is obviously very personal: something I'm working through. But there's some of it that... I like to understand the people around me and try to dissect and analyze it.

TJ: I wanted to create a world that I could go into and write from. In that world, I could control the exterior and what was pushing down on me. That control was very helpful in the creative process. Where, in reality -- where we are -- I can't really control that. How people perceive it, or what pressures are being applied to what types of songs should be written, and what type of record should be written, and…

**ZL: How people feel about it.**

TJ: Yeah, what decisions we should make, and what shows we should play, and whether or not we should do live TV, and all the stuff that I don't particularly enjoy.

**ZL: You lived that life -- _really_ lived inside that world as much as you probably could stomach -- on the last album. Because _Blurryface_ was… It kind of makes sense. Because I feel like _Trench_ -- as you said before, to some degree -- it’s a geographical play. It's like you've created a world. Blurryface was a character. So you had to go front that.**

**ZL: How did you feel at the end of that experience? Because I think fans will want to know. They loved the way that you announced your hiatus. It's always funny how you have to announce hiatuses these days, right?**

TJ: Which we never called it a hiatus, it just kind of...

**ZL: But that’s what we do, we just picked that term up, right?**

TJ: You guys picked that name, yeah.

**ZL: We have to just be like, “We gotta call it something!” Can’t call it a holiday, right? Being a musician is a holiday.**

TJ: Doesn’t a hiatus kind of say that Josh and I were sick of each other? Isn’t that what that kind of means?

**ZL: A hiatus is always the step before a split. It's like an intervention.**

TJ: Yeah. That's not what happened, but if that's what we're calling it, that’s fine.

**ZL: Yeah, so what went wrong with you guys? [laughs]**

TJ: Yeah. [laughs] We didn’t see eye-to-eye on anything.

## (04:49) “Heathens”[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: You seem to have a great relationship. I guess that -- even at the end of all that touring -- I mean, you tell me how it all felt at the end of the _Blurryface_ campaign, with “Heathens” thrown on top.**

TJ: After I had done... I wrote _Blurryface_. We released it. We started touring it a bunch. I couldn't... There was something... Sometimes it's hard to start creating. It's kind of like a muscle you have to work out.

TJ: Well, when the “Heathens” thing came up, I kind of took that as an exercise, like, “Let me just get something going. Give me a reason to write right now. Because I have a lot to say, but I just can't. Everything I turn to, every progression, every sample just feels uninspired to me right now.”

TJ: This idea came up. “Well, there’s this movie coming out.” I didn't know much about the movie. And, you know, “They want to know if you would write a song for it.” Like, “Well, I don't know. That's not really... I've never done anything like that before.”

TJ: Then they showed me a few scenes. They said, “We want you to do either a shoot-'em-up Will Smith song or a twisted love song between the Joker and Harley Quinn.” Neither of those things struck me as--

TJ: I was like, “You know, I'm just gonna write a song that I feel like is probably gonna be for the next record, or at least be for our fans. With my own twist on, “If I were meeting with those villains and I was bringing someone along” -- like a bring your friend to work day -- “what kind of conversation would I have in the car before I got in there?”

TJ: In a sense, if this song were to -- Well, we kind of got shoved into the mainstream. I felt like I always wanted to explain to the mainstream audience about our fans, and who we really are. And try to bring them along, and go, “Listen. This is what you should expect. Tread lightly. But we're powerful and these kids have something to say. They're worth listening to.”

TJ: So that song became something that I wanted to write to explain our dynamic with our fans, thinking that it would in no way fall in line with the movie. And then it did, and then it took off from there. So, it was a good exercise to get things flowing.

**ZL: And did it? After that, did you feel inspired?**

TJ: Yeah. I started writing more. A lot of ideas.

**ZL: Strange hit.**

TJ: The chorus was initially... The chorus melody was the verse melody. I just didn't feel like it was moving around the changes like it should. I remember, I showed Josh and a couple other guys on the road when I was just demoing it on my laptop. All I had was the verse and just the beat and the vibe. Like, “I gotta find a chorus.”

TJ: A few minutes after I'd showed them, we're getting ready for the show, and I hear someone. I still don't know who it was. It's one of the four or five guys that I was showing stuff to. They whistled the melody of what I _thought_ was the verse, down the hall as I was getting ready. And that's when I was like, “That’s the chorus.”

## (08:23) The Fans Wrote _Trench_[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: So, how do we get to _Trench_, Tyler? How do you go from a character-based concept into something which is an entire world? Which requires so much more fleshing out? And so much more color, and the videos require so much more commitment, and everything else?**

TJ: You asked earlier, “How was it to take a break -- the hiatus?” And to step away for what is now, I guess, a year. Honestly, the moment our last show -- which was here in Columbus -- it's our final show of the entire cycle. I went home and I started coming up with this world.

TJ: It started to consume me. It was all I could think about. I know every aspect of this world. I know what the weather's like in this world. I wanted to go there and write from that place. This studio then became, in a sense, my version of it.

TJ: I really wanted to dive deeper into the narrative of who Blurryface is. Not just to me, but who he's become. It's always probably very true, but it seemed a little cliche to say, “We wouldn't be here without our fans. This is about our fans. It wouldn't _be_ without them.” But I don't think they know how much _they've_ written the narrative. And how much of a back-and-forth we've been having without them even being fully aware.

TJ: This record is… They really did help write it. This thing wouldn't be breathing without them. They helped create this world, as well.

**ZL: How do you absorb that influence? Because you can see it when you're on a stage and you can hear it when you have a chance to meet them and talk to them about it.**

TJ: How do I hear them?

**ZL: Yeah. Like, are they taking --**

TJ: It is the Internet, man.

**ZL: Yeah?**

TJ: Yeah, I'm around.

**ZL: And they’re fleshing it out. They’re taking _Blurryface_, and they’re writing things about it, and they're adding to it and moving things around.**

TJ: Yeah.

**ZL: I mean, that's just incredible. That's like creative collaboration in real time.**

TJ: The character of Blurryface was this person to me that I was trying to confront. But then -- as the record cycle went on, and as I saw him come to life through other people's perspective, and our fans, the way that they viewed him -- it drove me to agree with them on how he's perceived.

**ZL: How’s he changed? How's it changed?**

TJ: If you go back to what Blurryface was representing at the time, it’s that mirror that -- I call it a seat at the table -- that you can star

## Transcripts/2018/Zane Lowe (Trench)

_See also: [2018 interviews](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Interviews/2018 "Interviews/2018")_

Zane Lowe of Apple Music Beats 1 Radio interviewed [Tyler Joseph](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Tyler_Joseph "Tyler Joseph") about [Trench](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Trench "Trench") in his studio basement. [[1]](https://youtu.be/s4CLo1gpHyQ) This interview was posted to YouTube on September 5, 2018, exactly one month before the record was released to the public. Aside from a brief interview with [Josh](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Josh_Dun "Josh Dun") the day after the release of [Jumpsuit](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Jumpsuit "Jumpsuit"),[[2]](https://youtu.be/pvWecLRFr3E) this was [Twenty One Pilots](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Twenty_One_Pilots "Twenty One Pilots")'s first interview following [The Hiatus](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/The_Hiatus "The Hiatus"); it was the first time either band member publicly dove into the story and inspiration behind _Trench_.

**Zane Lowe: This is the Batcave.**

Tyler Joseph: I've never really shown anyone this spot.

**ZL: Thanks for having us. Thanks for welcoming us. It's good to see you.**

TJ: Thanks for coming all the way to my place.

**ZL: It's a pleasure. It's lovely to be here. It's my first time, actually, in this part in the Midwest. Being out here, I realized, wow, isolation plays such a big part in your creative spirit, right?**

TJ: The isolation helps when creating something. I think that people would assume that the pressure of making another record to follow something that was considered a big moment for us in our career would be the pressure, when really it's the tiny comments that I think about.

TJ: Like when a friend's mom says, “I love your last record. I could just press play and listen to the whole thing as I worked out.” Something tiny like that, when I'm working on a song, will all of a sudden, like, “Can they work out to this?” It's the tiny little comments about the music and the decisions made in it that -- if I let too much of that in -- it can completely affect whether I turn left or right.

**ZL: Well, look, it's really great to be here, man, in your studio -- in your space where this new album has been made. I know that this is a particularly intense moment for us to catch up. Because normally what happens is, I catch up with an artist like yourself after a few weeks of decompression when the album’s done.**

**ZL: But I sort of snuck up on you -- and did this deliberately. Because when I heard the music, the idea of coming here and seeing you the day the album got done, that seed was planted. Because I realized that you had gone so deep in on the ideas, the concepts, and the entire complete thought of this album. I wanted to get you at its most raw. That's literally right now, right?**

TJ: Right now. Yeah, I'm pretty tired. Every moment away from a song is very valuable because the fresh ears aspect of it.

**ZL: How was that break that you took? Necessary?**

TJ: It was very necessary. A lot of the last album cycle, there was a lot of traveling.

**ZL: Well, you caught lightning in a bottle. I mean, you had to, right? It was -- you had to go. You had to go, go, go.**

TJ: Yeah. The schedule was very unpredictable. You know, “This is the next thing we need to do to capitalize on the momentum.” This time around I'm looking forward to a little more structure. We know what to expect a little bit more, which is fantastic.

**ZL: And yet you find yourself -- from what I've heard of this album, which is the whole thing thus far -- is that you have chosen this opportunity to dive _deeper_.**

TJ: I love stories. I love being able to dive into a story and write from that perspective. A lot of my writing is obviously very personal: something I'm working through. But there's some of it that... I like to understand the people around me and try to dissect and analyze it.

TJ: I wanted to create a world that I could go into and write from. In that world, I could control the exterior and what was pushing down on me. That control was very helpful in the creative process. Where, in reality -- where we are -- I can't really control that. How people perceive it, or what pressures are being applied to what types of songs should be written, and what type of record should be written, and…

**ZL: How people feel about it.**

TJ: Yeah, what decisions we should make, and what shows we should play, and whether or not we should do live TV, and all the stuff that I don't particularly enjoy.

**ZL: You lived that life -- _really_ lived inside that world as much as you probably could stomach -- on the last album. Because _Blurryface_ was… It kind of makes sense. Because I feel like _Trench_ -- as you said before, to some degree -- it’s a geographical play. It's like you've created a world. Blurryface was a character. So you had to go front that.**

**ZL: How did you feel at the end of that experience? Because I think fans will want to know. They loved the way that you announced your hiatus. It's always funny how you have to announce hiatuses these days, right?**

TJ: Which we never called it a hiatus, it just kind of...

**ZL: But that’s what we do, we just picked that term up, right?**

TJ: You guys picked that name, yeah.

**ZL: We have to just be like, “We gotta call it something!” Can’t call it a holiday, right? Being a musician is a holiday.**

TJ: Doesn’t a hiatus kind of say that Josh and I were sick of each other? Isn’t that what that kind of means?

**ZL: A hiatus is always the step before a split. It's like an intervention.**

TJ: Yeah. That's not what happened, but if that's what we're calling it, that’s fine.

**ZL: Yeah, so what went wrong with you guys? [laughs]**

TJ: Yeah. [laughs] We didn’t see eye-to-eye on anything.

## (04:49) “Heathens”[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: You seem to have a great relationship. I guess that -- even at the end of all that touring -- I mean, you tell me how it all felt at the end of the _Blurryface_ campaign, with “Heathens” thrown on top.**

TJ: After I had done... I wrote _Blurryface_. We released it. We started touring it a bunch. I couldn't... There was something... Sometimes it's hard to start creating. It's kind of like a muscle you have to work out.

TJ: Well, when the “Heathens” thing came up, I kind of took that as an exercise, like, “Let me just get something going. Give me a reason to write right now. Because I have a lot to say, but I just can't. Everything I turn to, every progression, every sample just feels uninspired to me right now.”

TJ: This idea came up. “Well, there’s this movie coming out.” I didn't know much about the movie. And, you know, “They want to know if you would write a song for it.” Like, “Well, I don't know. That's not really... I've never done anything like that before.”

TJ: Then they showed me a few scenes. They said, “We want you to do either a shoot-'em-up Will Smith song or a twisted love song between the Joker and Harley Quinn.” Neither of those things struck me as--

TJ: I was like, “You know, I'm just gonna write a song that I feel like is probably gonna be for the next record, or at least be for our fans. With my own twist on, “If I were meeting with those villains and I was bringing someone along” -- like a bring your friend to work day -- “what kind of conversation would I have in the car before I got in there?”

TJ: In a sense, if this song were to -- Well, we kind of got shoved into the mainstream. I felt like I always wanted to explain to the mainstream audience about our fans, and who we really are. And try to bring them along, and go, “Listen. This is what you should expect. Tread lightly. But we're powerful and these kids have something to say. They're worth listening to.”

TJ: So that song became something that I wanted to write to explain our dynamic with our fans, thinking that it would in no way fall in line with the movie. And then it did, and then it took off from there. So, it was a good exercise to get things flowing.

**ZL: And did it? After that, did you feel inspired?**

TJ: Yeah. I started writing more. A lot of ideas.

**ZL: Strange hit.**

TJ: The chorus was initially... The chorus melody was the verse melody. I just didn't feel like it was moving around the changes like it should. I remember, I showed Josh and a couple other guys on the road when I was just demoing it on my laptop. All I had was the verse and just the beat and the vibe. Like, “I gotta find a chorus.”

TJ: A few minutes after I'd showed them, we're getting ready for the show, and I hear someone. I still don't know who it was. It's one of the four or five guys that I was showing stuff to. They whistled the melody of what I _thought_ was the verse, down the hall as I was getting ready. And that's when I was like, “That’s the chorus.”

## (08:23) The Fans Wrote _Trench_[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: So, how do we get to _Trench_, Tyler? How do you go from a character-based concept into something which is an entire world? Which requires so much more fleshing out? And so much more color, and the videos require so much more commitment, and everything else?**

TJ: You asked earlier, “How was it to take a break -- the hiatus?” And to step away for what is now, I guess, a year. Honestly, the moment our last show -- which was here in Columbus -- it's our final show of the entire cycle. I went home and I started coming up with this world.

TJ: It started to consume me. It was all I could think about. I know every aspect of this world. I know what the weather's like in this world. I wanted to go there and write from that place. This studio then became, in a sense, my version of it.

TJ: I really wanted to dive deeper into the narrative of who Blurryface is. Not just to me, but who he's become. It's always probably very true, but it seemed a little cliche to say, “We wouldn't be here without our fans. This is about our fans. It wouldn't _be_ without them.” But I don't think they know how much _they've_ written the narrative. And how much of a back-and-forth we've been having without them even being fully aware.

TJ: This record is… They really did help write it. This thing wouldn't be breathing without them. They helped create this world, as well.

**ZL: How do you absorb that influence? Because you can see it when you're on a stage and you can hear it when you have a chance to meet them and talk to them about it.**

TJ: How do I hear them?

**ZL: Yeah. Like, are they taking --**

TJ: It is the Internet, man.

**ZL: Yeah?**

TJ: Yeah, I'm around.

**ZL: And they’re fleshing it out. They’re taking _Blurryface_, and they’re writing things about it, and they're adding to it and moving things around.**

TJ: Yeah.

**ZL: I mean, that's just incredible. That's like creative collaboration in real time.**

TJ: The character of Blurryface was this person to me that I was trying to confront. But then -- as the record cycle went on, and as I saw him come to life through other people's perspective, and our fans, the way that they viewed him -- it drove me to agree with them on how he's perceived.

**ZL: How’s he changed? How's it changed?**

TJ: If you go back to what Blurryface was representing at the time, it’s that mirror that -- I call it a seat at the table -- that you can star

The Zane Lowe Trench interview has excellent quotes: "I wanted to create a world that I could go into and write from" and "I know every aspect of this world. I know what the weather's like in this world." Also the Heathens chorus story (verse melody became the chorus).

Let me get one more slice (offset 50000) for more on the writing process in the basement and "Leave the City". Then do the remaining fact-check searches (Overcompensate Hot 100 peak, The Craving chart, "3 minute 20 second" quote, "pore over" method, "Level of Concern" #23).

# Transcripts/2018/Zane Lowe (Trench)

e across and really understand. Everyone knows what they don't like about themselves. But how do you compensate for that? What are you doing because you don't like that? Trying to understand that and maybe fix that.

TJ: Then I realized that it's all about jurisdiction. There's certain places that I'll be -- whether it's mentally or physically -- where he has jurisdiction. If I can try to leave those places -- if I can try to stay away from those places -- then he starts to lose a little more of a grip and control of me. That's what Trench was, and what it is.

TJ: It helped me compartmentalize in my mind where I need to try to leave. And get to somewhere that's safer and a little more unpredictable, a little more wild, much more creative, a little scarier, a little bit of an abyss. But you don’t have to play by his rules. That's helped.

## (12:39) Starting to Write Music[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: I wonder when you realized that you were different. You thought about things different and things settled with you differently. At what point in your life you realized that you were gonna have to develop some tools in order to function and live with the person that you are?**

TJ: I never would have turned to music if I didn't feel like I needed to work on something or change or cope with something. I think that I was perfectly fine before music. And then something happened, where I felt a buildup of some sort. I didn't know how to release that. I didn't know how to decompress that and to have an outlet for it.

TJ: I was forced to learn how to play the piano, at least the way I look at it. I grew up sharing a bedroom with my brother. He would tell you. We both love music, but there was something that happened where I realized, “Okay, I can say anything I want now.” When I first showed my parents a song or two, I was really concerned that they were going to be really concerned.

**ZL: How’d your parents take it?**

TJ: Well, that's what was so surprising about it. When I was concerned about... It felt like when I was writing a song and I would show someone, that was like, “Okay, now let's start the conversation.” But what would usually have been the beginning of a long conversation/check up-on-you/lecture was just, “Wow, that's great.” And that was it. That was the end of the conversation. That’s when I was like, “I can do this _more_.”

**ZL: Yeah, the relief.**

TJ: Like, “I don't have to keep on talking about it afterwards.”

**ZL: What role did your faith play in that when you were growing up? Trying to be the person that you grew up being, and also growing into being a young adult, and wanting to be an artist, and wanting that freedom -- that flexibility to touch on subjects. Because you've got to get out of your system, right? I could see that that could create a conflict if it wasn’t managed right.**

TJ: I have this theory about leapfrogging in generations. I think it can apply to faith. It can apply to wealth. There's this constant overcompensation and then compensating that.

TJ: My parents grew up in an environment where there wasn't any talk of faith or any sort of religion. Then they both had a moment where they became Christians when they were in their college age. So when they got married and wanted to raise kids, they were like, “We want to raise a family that has faith and believes in God and instill that.”

TJ: What I believe about God and my faith, I would say, is very different from them. But I think it's a lesson in knowing that what I believe is different from _everyone_. Even my mom and my dad -- people who formed me. They _should_, in theory, have the closest version of it, but it's so different, even that. I think it's actually made my faith stronger in the version that I believe and I hold on to.

TJ: This music -- I'm trying to create and trying to answer those questions. I'm throwing those questions out that I felt like weren't supposed to be asked. But when I asked it in a song, my parents just said, “It's great.” That was such a big moment for me. And so yeah my faith is constantly playing a part in the music that I write.

## (16:50) Popping Your Head Out of the Ground[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: As I said at the very beginning of our conversation, you're so tucked away in here. I can see why you would continue to work and create and work and create, because it's a very protective place. It feels literally like you're about five stories under the ground.**

TJ: Bomb shelter.

**ZL: Yeah, it does. I wonder what it's like when you pop your head up above ground, for you. What life's like?**

TJ: Let's talk about the “popping the head out of the ground,” because that's actually a phrase Josh and I have used to describe the part of our career that we just don't remember. “Wait, how did you guys all of a sudden do our version of making it or getting people's attention?”

TJ: We see all these bands around us -- I'm talking about the local scene, back eight, nine years ago -- we see all these other bands around us. “Should we do what they're doing? Should we try to follow their lead? Should we…?” And we decided, “You know what? Let's just go underground.”

TJ: We went underground and we came up with a show. Then we -- with our head down -- we just started saying, “Yes to that show. Yes, let's play that. Let's play that. Let's play that. Let's do that. Let's create this.” Head is down. And then, all of a sudden, we came up and we had a record deal. We were doing a headline tour. It was like, “Man, how did that happen?”

TJ: I realized the importance of isolation and just honing in on something. Not letting in “what are they doing” or “should we follow that” or “does that change our decision, now that they did that?” Just kind of diving in and going for it, and then coming up and realizing, “Wow, we're five miles ahead of those other bands that we were just looking at.”

## (18:39) Josh[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D7&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: What role does Josh play in all this, for you -- outside of being an amazing drummer and being one half of the band, everything else -- but on a human level? You guys have got a lot of similarities, but also, you seem like different people, which is good.**

TJ: I think, in the live show especially, there's been some shows where, “Man, I don't feel like I should be up here right now. I don't feel good enough. I don't feel like what I'm doing is considered good.” But there’s just been so many times when I look over at Josh and he's just ripping, man. And it just shocks my system. And then I walk downstage and then square my shoulders up to the audience.

TJ: There's only really been one show where it happened to him and me. We got offstage and we were just like, “What just happened?”

**ZL: Did you know at the time that it was happening?**

TJ: Yeah. It was a festival. I think it would have been like 2013. It was one of our first times doing a festival in Europe. It may have been Pukkelpop. So we got onto a main stage. We were like, “Oh my gosh. We got main stage at like 3 p.m. That’s crazy.”

TJ: And you realize, “Oh okay, this is a scheduling thing.” Rightfully so. This is our first time in that country. There's no reason why we should have had an audience. But when you get ready to play a show, you kind of like, “I wonder who's gonna be there.”

TJ: I always assume no one's gonna be there, just to get myself ready, but I wasn't ready for the _empty_ field. That field was so much bigger with -- people will think, “Look how many people are there when it's full.” It's like, “This field is ginormous.” Yeah? Now wait until everyone's _gone_. Then you realize how big that field is.

## (20:30) Fans Building the Record[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D8&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: It must be interesting finishing the record and watching people get it right or get it wrong in real time. Are you even reading what people are saying?**

TJ: They are also building the world, like I said. We’re very… Not to come off as on that stalker level, but I do watch them. I see how... I don't watch everyone, though. I watch the ones that really get it, really understand.

**ZL: So you have specific fans that you--**

TJ: Not specific -- I mean, it's a group of them. There's this outer layer noise that I consider to be not relevant. But what does that fan that really understands and has tracked with me up until this point -- how is this hitting them? And the story builds from there, man.

TJ: We'll see if this works, by the way. You're pitting this idea of a concept and the story. It's very thought-out. There's a bunch of time spent in between release and... I don't even know if this is going to work in the day of streaming and getting a single out every chance you can.

## (21:47) Mental Health[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D9&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: When you guys first came out, people didn't understand the depth of subject matter and what you were really trying to say. They were focusing on the melodies and the music and the beats and the production and the live shows and all the things that make a surface impression.**

**ZL: Over the course of all your albums now we’ve found you going deeper and deeper and saying, “Look, there are fundamental things I'm trying to fix here, or I'm trying to understand.”**

**ZL: Now more than ever, we're all trying to understand those things. We're all having louder conversations about anxiety, depression, lack of self-worth. We're speaking as one a lot more clearly about that, because I think that that's pretty accepted. That's a good way of trying to demystify it. Do you know what I mean?**

TJ: We're getting that right.

**ZL: We're getting that right?**

TJ: This is moving in the right direction, for sure.

**ZL: It's something that you experience. I'm taking a punt on that, listening to your music.**

TJ: The fact that we're now in a world where we're talking about it is something that I've been looking for for a while. I'm really glad that we're here. I'm proud of our culture in that way, for sure. [pause] I mean, suicide, too. You know, we like to name the depression and the anxiety…

**ZL: You’re right. We’re terrified of that word.**

TJ: Yeah. We gotta say that too, you know? It's finally... We're talking about it. It's a thing. My mom's a schoolteacher. I talk with her all the time about the things that she looks out for and how it affects that environment, as its own microcosm of a culture. It's important to talk about. That it's real.

**ZL: How real can it get for you?**

TJ: I've always been pretty good at compartmentalizing. There's nothing... It's not because I had to cope with something or whatever. I think that I was maybe born with being able to compartmentalize. I think my music is the only real, true window into a compartment that I… That’s about as comfortable as I like to get with diving into something that is still breathing, moving, shifting, adapting, becoming immune.

TJ: As much as the conversation about it is very good, there's something about the personal aspect of it that is very good to make sure that it doesn't take life, and doesn't gain traction and breathe oxygen. And so, my music is me talking about it. It's the window into it. But I don't think it's healthy for me to give you the keys to that house.

## (25:02) “Leave the City”[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D10&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: The reason I reached on my phone was because I'm looking at the track listing. I wanted to talk about... We've talked about the first song. I want to talk about the last song. I want to talk about “Leave the City.”**

**ZL: I want to talk about the restrained weight that's in that song. How it never quite reaches the crescendo, and it always promises, but doesn't quite get there. And at the end, it’s just, it’s like… I mean, you tell me what the last word on the album is. The last words. There's an isolated sentence.**

TJ: “They know what I mean.”

**ZL: Yeah. “They know what I mean.”**

TJ: That song, not only is it inside of the narrative, but in that narrative, I know that I need to leave somewhere and start this journey -- this point in between two places that a lot of us can find ourselves in. Whatever version of that fits into your life, we're always trying to dance in between those two places.

TJ: How do we get there? It's scary and you don't know what to expect. It's hard to see. But this record is about pushing through and starting that. Starting that journey between those two places. I just start it.

TJ: I would never… In this record, I did not define what “where you're supposed to be” is, though. There's no name for it. That's not defined. That was intentional to be a part of this process. I knew this record was about getting up and starting that. I'm not going to find that thing in this record yet.

TJ: And that's what the song “Leave the City” does. It gets you there and then it doesn't… It kind of drops you off and like, “Okay.”

## (26:42) Jenna[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D11&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: You're about to embark on another tour -- and all the things that come with making music and reaching your fans -- but “Leave the City” could take you anywhere, right? Do you even…?**

TJ: What's next?

**ZL: What's next? And is it even music? Did you enjoy that year off? I mean you've got an amazing house. You're married. I said to Jenna, your wife -- who’s lovely, by the way --**

TJ: She's, um… I just want to get it on the record. [pause] Can I talk about her for a second?

**ZL: One hundred percent!**

TJ: Okay. Starting this career felt like I was standing at the edge of an ocean and I was given some supplies. They were like, “Okay, make a boat.” I put this thing together, and I wrapped it up, and I built this boat enough to start to float. We started going and found some more debris on the way and kind of built this thing. Then, before you know it, I'm in this tugboat-sized thing. It's got a motor and we're going. Then eventually things happen and I'm on a yacht. And we're just flying through this journey.

TJ: All the while, I think that some people would assume that my significant other in the process is in a smaller boat next to me, waiting for this boat to inevitably either wreck or run out of fuel. And when it does, I hop on to hers and we head off into the sunset.

TJ: When actually, what's happening is -- in relation to who she is to me, I've built this little tugboat thing. That's about as big as it ever got. And she is waiting for me to run out of gas in a cruise ship. And when [the tugboat] goes down, I've got _this_ to pick me up.

TJ: That’s just a really weird way of saying that she's the best thing I've accomplished and I can't wait to just... lean on her.

**ZL: Oof, there you go! There you go. Alright. “I can't wait.” Those are great words.**

TJ: And maybe that'll inspire the next record.

**ZL: Oh, there he is! He's pulling it back from the brink of absolute disaster. That was the moment where it all came out right there. But understandably so. On the last day of the album, you're like -- and remember what I said about flirting with finality? Artists who... What's the obsession with finality?**

TJ: Yeah.

**ZL: You have this life. You have this other boat. And yet you choose to stay on the tugboat, then.**

## (29:32) Glorify Getting Old[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D12&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**Are you unafraid of living a different life?**

TJ: I think that...

**ZL: You’d be amazed how many musicians are _afraid_ of stopping.**

TJ: I think what helps me is to glorify getting old, not be afraid of it. I'm looking forward to it. I think that if our culture were to see our elderly in that way, as like... They've accomplished something. They ran a race and they have a _lot_ to tell us about how we could better run it. I think that that would help with a lot of things.

**ZL: Have you always felt that way? Is that why you put two old people on the cover of _Vessel_?**

TJ: Yeah, I've always felt that way. Actually, my grandfather, who's on that cover, died last month. But he was a big part of my life. I think more so now, after his passing, do I realize how much of a resource I had. I have one grandfather who's still living, who's absolutely still an inspiration to me.

**ZL: Ask the questions.**

TJ: You know, he’s a… He's dealt with alcoholism his whole life and he's been sober for so many years now.

**ZL: You've never drunk, right?**

TJ: No.

**ZL: Yeah? Being on the road and all that stuff, never felt the pull toward…? It just doesn't--**

TJ: I've had one. I've had -- Do you want to ask me about my first alcoholic beverage?

**ZL: One hundred percent.**

TJ: It was an expired Bud Light. I was like probably 13.

**ZL: That's it?**

TJ: And it was terrible. In a way I think it's a blessing.

**ZL: It's a blessing!**

TJ: Yeah, I had to chase it with Gatorade. It was awful.

## (31:22) Living in the Basement[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D13&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: I’m excited, man. [sets phone on desk]**

TJ: [watching the phone slide] Nope, nope, nope. [the phone falls on the floor] Told you. It's a slanted table. [someone offscreen cracks up] Why do you think I have all these gigantic mouse pads over here?

**ZL: [picking up his phone and standing up] Dude, this is the most pristine and clean, amazing…**

TJ: I gotta be honest with you…

**ZL: Don't tell me you cleaned it for us.**

TJ: Jenna dusted this before you guys came.

**ZL: Have you been literally sitting in here in your pants -- like in your boxer shorts -- literally just stinking up the joint? Did you grow a beard?**

TJ: I -- yeah.

**ZL: You did grow a beard?**

TJ: Yeah, I did. I shaved last night.

**ZL: Get out of here! You had a beard? How deep it go?**

TJ: It was terrible, man.

**ZL: No, how committed were you?**

TJ: It was so itchy and I hated it.

**ZL: Was it long?**

TJ: It wasn't. It was stringy.

**ZL: It was like your first real beard?**

TJ: It was not…

**ZL: It would’ve looked terrible.**

TJ: It was a shame.

**ZL: You’ve got to _culture_ a beard. You can't just grow it out and think you’re gonna look like Rick Rubin. That takes decades of planning.**

TJ: I know. There's so many more things I need to go through in my life before I can really commit.

**ZL: Puberty?**

TJ: Yeah, puberty’s one of them.

**ZL: So many things you’ve got to experience for the very first time. [gestures at Tyler’s shorts] Trousers. At some point you’ve got to put those on, yeah? See how they feel.**

TJ: I didn't shower for a long time. There was a moment where I hadn't looked in the mirror in

like a week. You should try that. It's crazy.

**ZL: Oh my god, what did you notice the first time you looked at yourself?**

TJ: I felt like I was getting older.

**ZL: Wow. So you noticed the change, cus you weren’t --**

TJ: Yeah, in a week. I was like, “yeah.” Maybe I was just really tired.

**ZL: That actually makes sense if you haven't noticed anything. What were you eating? You were being fed, obviously.**

TJ: Yeah, I mean, Jenna was --

**ZL: Taking care of you.**

TJ: She's a culinary artist.

**ZL: Was she ever concerned? Did she ever come down and just pat you on the shoulder, like, “You gotta get some sleep.”**

TJ: Yeah. She told me, like, “You should eat.” She's never too particular about hygiene, but she did several times, like “When’s the last time you took a shower?” Just those types of questions.

## (33:11) A Chance to Reflect[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D14&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: What an amazing time in your life, man. To be able to have achieved all of this and know you still have fuel in the tank to make your own most ambitious album and project to date. Most people settle here and then there's a compromise somewhere along the line. There's no compromise going on your art, and yet you've already gotten to this place.**

**ZL: As a way of saying goodbye, I wonder if you ever allow yourself -- probably not in the last 12 months -- but if at any point, you allow yourself a chance to reflect finally on where you're at in your life? Because how old are you now, Tyler?**

TJ: Twenty-nine.

**ZL: You’re twenty-nine years old, right? Are you scared of feeling reflective or feeling satisfied?**

TJ: I love creating. I need to create. But there's something about -- when it gets to this level -- there's something about convincing yourself that it's kind of not real. It's something that will go away. And preparing yourself.

TJ: I know that you talk about finality being something that artists are obsessed with, but I think that you have to try to get okay with that. The quicker you do, the more you'll enjoy this moment. I’m not --

**ZL: Do you know what ends that? Do you know what cures that?**

TJ: What?

**ZL: The end of narcissism. And you know what kills narcissism? Kids.**

TJ: I can't wait to have kids, man.

**ZL: Yeah.**

TJ: It's one more cycle.

**ZL: It's been great hanging, man. Thanks for letting us in.**

TJ: Thanks for coming.

# Transcripts/2018/Zane Lowe (Trench)

e across and really understand. Everyone knows what they don't like about themselves. But how do you compensate for that? What are you doing because you don't like that? Trying to understand that and maybe fix that.

TJ: Then I realized that it's all about jurisdiction. There's certain places that I'll be -- whether it's mentally or physically -- where he has jurisdiction. If I can try to leave those places -- if I can try to stay away from those places -- then he starts to lose a little more of a grip and control of me. That's what Trench was, and what it is.

TJ: It helped me compartmentalize in my mind where I need to try to leave. And get to somewhere that's safer and a little more unpredictable, a little more wild, much more creative, a little scarier, a little bit of an abyss. But you don’t have to play by his rules. That's helped.

## (12:39) Starting to Write Music[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: I wonder when you realized that you were different. You thought about things different and things settled with you differently. At what point in your life you realized that you were gonna have to develop some tools in order to function and live with the person that you are?**

TJ: I never would have turned to music if I didn't feel like I needed to work on something or change or cope with something. I think that I was perfectly fine before music. And then something happened, where I felt a buildup of some sort. I didn't know how to release that. I didn't know how to decompress that and to have an outlet for it.

TJ: I was forced to learn how to play the piano, at least the way I look at it. I grew up sharing a bedroom with my brother. He would tell you. We both love music, but there was something that happened where I realized, “Okay, I can say anything I want now.” When I first showed my parents a song or two, I was really concerned that they were going to be really concerned.

**ZL: How’d your parents take it?**

TJ: Well, that's what was so surprising about it. When I was concerned about... It felt like when I was writing a song and I would show someone, that was like, “Okay, now let's start the conversation.” But what would usually have been the beginning of a long conversation/check up-on-you/lecture was just, “Wow, that's great.” And that was it. That was the end of the conversation. That’s when I was like, “I can do this _more_.”

**ZL: Yeah, the relief.**

TJ: Like, “I don't have to keep on talking about it afterwards.”

**ZL: What role did your faith play in that when you were growing up? Trying to be the person that you grew up being, and also growing into being a young adult, and wanting to be an artist, and wanting that freedom -- that flexibility to touch on subjects. Because you've got to get out of your system, right? I could see that that could create a conflict if it wasn’t managed right.**

TJ: I have this theory about leapfrogging in generations. I think it can apply to faith. It can apply to wealth. There's this constant overcompensation and then compensating that.

TJ: My parents grew up in an environment where there wasn't any talk of faith or any sort of religion. Then they both had a moment where they became Christians when they were in their college age. So when they got married and wanted to raise kids, they were like, “We want to raise a family that has faith and believes in God and instill that.”

TJ: What I believe about God and my faith, I would say, is very different from them. But I think it's a lesson in knowing that what I believe is different from _everyone_. Even my mom and my dad -- people who formed me. They _should_, in theory, have the closest version of it, but it's so different, even that. I think it's actually made my faith stronger in the version that I believe and I hold on to.

TJ: This music -- I'm trying to create and trying to answer those questions. I'm throwing those questions out that I felt like weren't supposed to be asked. But when I asked it in a song, my parents just said, “It's great.” That was such a big moment for me. And so yeah my faith is constantly playing a part in the music that I write.

## (16:50) Popping Your Head Out of the Ground[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: As I said at the very beginning of our conversation, you're so tucked away in here. I can see why you would continue to work and create and work and create, because it's a very protective place. It feels literally like you're about five stories under the ground.**

TJ: Bomb shelter.

**ZL: Yeah, it does. I wonder what it's like when you pop your head up above ground, for you. What life's like?**

TJ: Let's talk about the “popping the head out of the ground,” because that's actually a phrase Josh and I have used to describe the part of our career that we just don't remember. “Wait, how did you guys all of a sudden do our version of making it or getting people's attention?”

TJ: We see all these bands around us -- I'm talking about the local scene, back eight, nine years ago -- we see all these other bands around us. “Should we do what they're doing? Should we try to follow their lead? Should we…?” And we decided, “You know what? Let's just go underground.”

TJ: We went underground and we came up with a show. Then we -- with our head down -- we just started saying, “Yes to that show. Yes, let's play that. Let's play that. Let's play that. Let's do that. Let's create this.” Head is down. And then, all of a sudden, we came up and we had a record deal. We were doing a headline tour. It was like, “Man, how did that happen?”

TJ: I realized the importance of isolation and just honing in on something. Not letting in “what are they doing” or “should we follow that” or “does that change our decision, now that they did that?” Just kind of diving in and going for it, and then coming up and realizing, “Wow, we're five miles ahead of those other bands that we were just looking at.”

## (18:39) Josh[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D7&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: What role does Josh play in all this, for you -- outside of being an amazing drummer and being one half of the band, everything else -- but on a human level? You guys have got a lot of similarities, but also, you seem like different people, which is good.**

TJ: I think, in the live show especially, there's been some shows where, “Man, I don't feel like I should be up here right now. I don't feel good enough. I don't feel like what I'm doing is considered good.” But there’s just been so many times when I look over at Josh and he's just ripping, man. And it just shocks my system. And then I walk downstage and then square my shoulders up to the audience.

TJ: There's only really been one show where it happened to him and me. We got offstage and we were just like, “What just happened?”

**ZL: Did you know at the time that it was happening?**

TJ: Yeah. It was a festival. I think it would have been like 2013. It was one of our first times doing a festival in Europe. It may have been Pukkelpop. So we got onto a main stage. We were like, “Oh my gosh. We got main stage at like 3 p.m. That’s crazy.”

TJ: And you realize, “Oh okay, this is a scheduling thing.” Rightfully so. This is our first time in that country. There's no reason why we should have had an audience. But when you get ready to play a show, you kind of like, “I wonder who's gonna be there.”

TJ: I always assume no one's gonna be there, just to get myself ready, but I wasn't ready for the _empty_ field. That field was so much bigger with -- people will think, “Look how many people are there when it's full.” It's like, “This field is ginormous.” Yeah? Now wait until everyone's _gone_. Then you realize how big that field is.

## (20:30) Fans Building the Record[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D8&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: It must be interesting finishing the record and watching people get it right or get it wrong in real time. Are you even reading what people are saying?**

TJ: They are also building the world, like I said. We’re very… Not to come off as on that stalker level, but I do watch them. I see how... I don't watch everyone, though. I watch the ones that really get it, really understand.

**ZL: So you have specific fans that you--**

TJ: Not specific -- I mean, it's a group of them. There's this outer layer noise that I consider to be not relevant. But what does that fan that really understands and has tracked with me up until this point -- how is this hitting them? And the story builds from there, man.

TJ: We'll see if this works, by the way. You're pitting this idea of a concept and the story. It's very thought-out. There's a bunch of time spent in between release and... I don't even know if this is going to work in the day of streaming and getting a single out every chance you can.

## (21:47) Mental Health[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D9&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: When you guys first came out, people didn't understand the depth of subject matter and what you were really trying to say. They were focusing on the melodies and the music and the beats and the production and the live shows and all the things that make a surface impression.**

**ZL: Over the course of all your albums now we’ve found you going deeper and deeper and saying, “Look, there are fundamental things I'm trying to fix here, or I'm trying to understand.”**

**ZL: Now more than ever, we're all trying to understand those things. We're all having louder conversations about anxiety, depression, lack of self-worth. We're speaking as one a lot more clearly about that, because I think that that's pretty accepted. That's a good way of trying to demystify it. Do you know what I mean?**

TJ: We're getting that right.

**ZL: We're getting that right?**

TJ: This is moving in the right direction, for sure.

**ZL: It's something that you experience. I'm taking a punt on that, listening to your music.**

TJ: The fact that we're now in a world where we're talking about it is something that I've been looking for for a while. I'm really glad that we're here. I'm proud of our culture in that way, for sure. [pause] I mean, suicide, too. You know, we like to name the depression and the anxiety…

**ZL: You’re right. We’re terrified of that word.**

TJ: Yeah. We gotta say that too, you know? It's finally... We're talking about it. It's a thing. My mom's a schoolteacher. I talk with her all the time about the things that she looks out for and how it affects that environment, as its own microcosm of a culture. It's important to talk about. That it's real.

**ZL: How real can it get for you?**

TJ: I've always been pretty good at compartmentalizing. There's nothing... It's not because I had to cope with something or whatever. I think that I was maybe born with being able to compartmentalize. I think my music is the only real, true window into a compartment that I… That’s about as comfortable as I like to get with diving into something that is still breathing, moving, shifting, adapting, becoming immune.

TJ: As much as the conversation about it is very good, there's something about the personal aspect of it that is very good to make sure that it doesn't take life, and doesn't gain traction and breathe oxygen. And so, my music is me talking about it. It's the window into it. But I don't think it's healthy for me to give you the keys to that house.

## (25:02) “Leave the City”[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D10&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: The reason I reached on my phone was because I'm looking at the track listing. I wanted to talk about... We've talked about the first song. I want to talk about the last song. I want to talk about “Leave the City.”**

**ZL: I want to talk about the restrained weight that's in that song. How it never quite reaches the crescendo, and it always promises, but doesn't quite get there. And at the end, it’s just, it’s like… I mean, you tell me what the last word on the album is. The last words. There's an isolated sentence.**

TJ: “They know what I mean.”

**ZL: Yeah. “They know what I mean.”**

TJ: That song, not only is it inside of the narrative, but in that narrative, I know that I need to leave somewhere and start this journey -- this point in between two places that a lot of us can find ourselves in. Whatever version of that fits into your life, we're always trying to dance in between those two places.

TJ: How do we get there? It's scary and you don't know what to expect. It's hard to see. But this record is about pushing through and starting that. Starting that journey between those two places. I just start it.

TJ: I would never… In this record, I did not define what “where you're supposed to be” is, though. There's no name for it. That's not defined. That was intentional to be a part of this process. I knew this record was about getting up and starting that. I'm not going to find that thing in this record yet.

TJ: And that's what the song “Leave the City” does. It gets you there and then it doesn't… It kind of drops you off and like, “Okay.”

## (26:42) Jenna[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D11&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: You're about to embark on another tour -- and all the things that come with making music and reaching your fans -- but “Leave the City” could take you anywhere, right? Do you even…?**

TJ: What's next?

**ZL: What's next? And is it even music? Did you enjoy that year off? I mean you've got an amazing house. You're married. I said to Jenna, your wife -- who’s lovely, by the way --**

TJ: She's, um… I just want to get it on the record. [pause] Can I talk about her for a second?

**ZL: One hundred percent!**

TJ: Okay. Starting this career felt like I was standing at the edge of an ocean and I was given some supplies. They were like, “Okay, make a boat.” I put this thing together, and I wrapped it up, and I built this boat enough to start to float. We started going and found some more debris on the way and kind of built this thing. Then, before you know it, I'm in this tugboat-sized thing. It's got a motor and we're going. Then eventually things happen and I'm on a yacht. And we're just flying through this journey.

TJ: All the while, I think that some people would assume that my significant other in the process is in a smaller boat next to me, waiting for this boat to inevitably either wreck or run out of fuel. And when it does, I hop on to hers and we head off into the sunset.

TJ: When actually, what's happening is -- in relation to who she is to me, I've built this little tugboat thing. That's about as big as it ever got. And she is waiting for me to run out of gas in a cruise ship. And when [the tugboat] goes down, I've got _this_ to pick me up.

TJ: That’s just a really weird way of saying that she's the best thing I've accomplished and I can't wait to just... lean on her.

**ZL: Oof, there you go! There you go. Alright. “I can't wait.” Those are great words.**

TJ: And maybe that'll inspire the next record.

**ZL: Oh, there he is! He's pulling it back from the brink of absolute disaster. That was the moment where it all came out right there. But understandably so. On the last day of the album, you're like -- and remember what I said about flirting with finality? Artists who... What's the obsession with finality?**

TJ: Yeah.

**ZL: You have this life. You have this other boat. And yet you choose to stay on the tugboat, then.**

## (29:32) Glorify Getting Old[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D12&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**Are you unafraid of living a different life?**

TJ: I think that...

**ZL: You’d be amazed how many musicians are _afraid_ of stopping.**

TJ: I think what helps me is to glorify getting old, not be afraid of it. I'm looking forward to it. I think that if our culture were to see our elderly in that way, as like... They've accomplished something. They ran a race and they have a _lot_ to tell us about how we could better run it. I think that that would help with a lot of things.

**ZL: Have you always felt that way? Is that why you put two old people on the cover of _Vessel_?**

TJ: Yeah, I've always felt that way. Actually, my grandfather, who's on that cover, died last month. But he was a big part of my life. I think more so now, after his passing, do I realize how much of a resource I had. I have one grandfather who's still living, who's absolutely still an inspiration to me.

**ZL: Ask the questions.**

TJ: You know, he’s a… He's dealt with alcoholism his whole life and he's been sober for so many years now.

**ZL: You've never drunk, right?**

TJ: No.

**ZL: Yeah? Being on the road and all that stuff, never felt the pull toward…? It just doesn't--**

TJ: I've had one. I've had -- Do you want to ask me about my first alcoholic beverage?

**ZL: One hundred percent.**

TJ: It was an expired Bud Light. I was like probably 13.

**ZL: That's it?**

TJ: And it was terrible. In a way I think it's a blessing.

**ZL: It's a blessing!**

TJ: Yeah, I had to chase it with Gatorade. It was awful.

## (31:22) Living in the Basement[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D13&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: I’m excited, man. [sets phone on desk]**

TJ: [watching the phone slide] Nope, nope, nope. [the phone falls on the floor] Told you. It's a slanted table. [someone offscreen cracks up] Why do you think I have all these gigantic mouse pads over here?

**ZL: [picking up his phone and standing up] Dude, this is the most pristine and clean, amazing…**

TJ: I gotta be honest with you…

**ZL: Don't tell me you cleaned it for us.**

TJ: Jenna dusted this before you guys came.

**ZL: Have you been literally sitting in here in your pants -- like in your boxer shorts -- literally just stinking up the joint? Did you grow a beard?**

TJ: I -- yeah.

**ZL: You did grow a beard?**

TJ: Yeah, I did. I shaved last night.

**ZL: Get out of here! You had a beard? How deep it go?**

TJ: It was terrible, man.

**ZL: No, how committed were you?**

TJ: It was so itchy and I hated it.

**ZL: Was it long?**

TJ: It wasn't. It was stringy.

**ZL: It was like your first real beard?**

TJ: It was not…

**ZL: It would’ve looked terrible.**

TJ: It was a shame.

**ZL: You’ve got to _culture_ a beard. You can't just grow it out and think you’re gonna look like Rick Rubin. That takes decades of planning.**

TJ: I know. There's so many more things I need to go through in my life before I can really commit.

**ZL: Puberty?**

TJ: Yeah, puberty’s one of them.

**ZL: So many things you’ve got to experience for the very first time. [gestures at Tyler’s shorts] Trousers. At some point you’ve got to put those on, yeah? See how they feel.**

TJ: I didn't shower for a long time. There was a moment where I hadn't looked in the mirror in

like a week. You should try that. It's crazy.

**ZL: Oh my god, what did you notice the first time you looked at yourself?**

TJ: I felt like I was getting older.

**ZL: Wow. So you noticed the change, cus you weren’t --**

TJ: Yeah, in a week. I was like, “yeah.” Maybe I was just really tired.

**ZL: That actually makes sense if you haven't noticed anything. What were you eating? You were being fed, obviously.**

TJ: Yeah, I mean, Jenna was --

**ZL: Taking care of you.**

TJ: She's a culinary artist.

**ZL: Was she ever concerned? Did she ever come down and just pat you on the shoulder, like, “You gotta get some sleep.”**

TJ: Yeah. She told me, like, “You should eat.” She's never too particular about hygiene, but she did several times, like “When’s the last time you took a shower?” Just those types of questions.

## (33:11) A Chance to Reflect[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Ftwentyonepilots.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FTranscripts%2F2018%2FZane_Lowe_%28Trench%29%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D14&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")]

**ZL: What an amazing time in your life, man. To be able to have achieved all of this and know you still have fuel in the tank to make your own most ambitious album and project to date. Most people settle here and then there's a compromise somewhere along the line. There's no compromise going on your art, and yet you've already gotten to this place.**

**ZL: As a way of saying goodbye, I wonder if you ever allow yourself -- probably not in the last 12 months -- but if at any point, you allow yourself a chance to reflect finally on where you're at in your life? Because how old are you now, Tyler?**

TJ: Twenty-nine.

**ZL: You’re twenty-nine years old, right? Are you scared of feeling reflective or feeling satisfied?**

TJ: I love creating. I need to create. But there's something about -- when it gets to this level -- there's something about convincing yourself that it's kind of not real. It's something that will go away. And preparing yourself.

TJ: I know that you talk about finality being something that artists are obsessed with, but I think that you have to try to get okay with that. The quicker you do, the more you'll enjoy this moment. I’m not --

**ZL: Do you know what ends that? Do you know what cures that?**

TJ: What?

**ZL: The end of narcissism. And you know what kills narcissism? Kids.**

TJ: I can't wait to have kids, man.

**ZL: Yeah.**

TJ: It's one more cycle.

**ZL: It's been great hanging, man. Thanks for letting us in.**

TJ: Thanks for coming.

## Transcripts/2021/BBCR1 Shy Away

_See also: [2021 interviews](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Interviews/2021 "Interviews/2021")_

On April 7, 2021, [Tyler Joseph](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Tyler_Joseph "Tyler Joseph") was interviewed by Jack Saunders with BBC Radio 1 about the new [Twenty One Pilots](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Twenty_One_Pilots "Twenty One Pilots") single "[Shy Away](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Shy_Away "Shy Away")" and the announcement of their forthcoming album, _[Scaled and Icy](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Scaled\_and\_Icy "Scaled and Icy")_. This transcript is cut together from the aired interview[[1]](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Transcripts/2021/BBCR1_Shy_Away#cite_note-interview-1), the article[[2]](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Transcripts/2021/BBCR1_Shy_Away#cite_note-article-2), and the tweet[[3]](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Transcripts/2021/BBCR1_Shy_Away#cite_note-tweet-3) that were each posted by BBC Radio 1. Each source contains quotes that the others did not have; the order of these mismatched quotes is unclear, so some text in this transcript may appear out of order. Quotes from the tweeted video and article are linked.

*   [1 Transcript](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Transcripts/2021/BBCR1_Shy_Away#Transcript)
    *   [1.1 Shy Away](https://twentyonepilots.fandom.com/wiki/Transcripts/2021/BBCR1_Shy_Away#Shy_Away)
